source_text: Ναί, φασίν· ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ σάρξ, ὥστε καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀναγκάζειν συναμαρτάνειν αὐτῇ, μάτην κατηγοροῦντες αὐτῆς καὶ τὰ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων ἁμαρτήματα μόνῃ περιτιθέντες. Ποῦ γὰρ καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἁμαρτῆσαι ἡ σὰρξ δυνήσεται, ἐὰν μὴ τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχῃ προηγουμένην καὶ προκαλουμένην αὐτήν; Ὥσπερ γὰρ ζεῦγος βοῶν λυθέντων ἀπ' ἀλλήλων τοῦ ζυγοῦ τῶν βοῶν οὐδέτερος αὐτῶν κατ' ἰδίαν ἀροῦν δύναται, οὕτως οὐδὲ ψυχὴ καὶ σῶμα λυθέντα τῆς συζυγίας καθ' ἑαυτὰ ποιῆσαί τι δύνανται. Eἰ δὲ καὶ ἡ σὰρξ μόνη ἁμαρτωλός, μόνης ταύτης ἕνεκεν ἦλθεν ὁ σωτήρ, καθώς φησιν· Oὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίους ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἰς μετάνοιαν. Ἐπειδὴ οὖν τιμία παρὰ θεῷ καὶ ἔνδοξος παρὰ πάντα τὰ ποιήματα δέδεικται ἡ σάρξ, δικαίως ἂν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ σωθήσεται. Λεκτέον οὖν πρὸς τοὺς λέγοντας ὅτι, εἰ καὶ τὰ μάλιστα τοῦ θεοῦ ποίημα τυγχάνει οὖσα καὶ τιμία αὐτῷ παρὰ πάντα, οὐκ εὐθέως καὶ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἔχει. Καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπον τὸ μετὰ τηλικαύτης βουλῆς γενόμενον καὶ παρὰ πάντα τὰ λοιπὰ τίμιον περιορᾶν τὸν ποιήσαντα εἰς τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι; Eἶτα ὁ μὲν πλάστης καὶ ζωγράφος, εἰ τὰς εἰκόνας, ἃς ἂν ποιήσωσι, διαμένειν ἐθέλουσιν, ἵνα δι' αὐτῶν δοξάζωνται, φθειρομένας αὐτὰς ἀνακαινοποιοῦσιν· ὁ δὲ θεὸς τὸ αὐτοῦ κτῆμα καὶ πλάσμα περιεῖδεν ἂν ὡς τὸ μὴ ὄν, μηκέτι δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸ εἶναι; Ματαιοπόνον ἀποκαλοῦμεν, ὥσπερ εἴ τις οἰκίαν οἰκοδομήσας ἔπειτα καταλύοι, ἢ καταλελυμένην περιορῴη, δυνάμενος ἀναστῆσαι· τὸν δὲ θεὸν οὐκ αἰτιασόμεθα, ὅτι μάτην ποιεῖ; Ἀλλ' οὐχ ὁ ἄφθαρτος τοιοῦτος, οὐκ ἄφρων ὁ τῶν ὅλων πέφυκε νοῦς. Eὐφημείτωσαν οἱ ἄπιστοι, εἰ τὸ μὴ πιστεύειν ἔχουσιν αὐτοί! Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ κέκληκεν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν καὶ ἐπαγγέλλεται τὴν αἰωνίαν ζωήν. Ἔνθα γὰρ τὸν ἄνθρωπον εὐαγγελίζεται σῶσαι, καὶ τῇ σαρκὶ εὐαγγελίζεται. Τί γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλ' ἢ τὸ ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος συνεστὸς ζῶον λογικόν; Μὴ οὖν καθ' ἑαυτὴν ψυχὴ ἄνθρωπος; Oὔκ· ἀλλ' ἀνθρώπου ψυχή. Μὴ οὖν καλοῖτο σῶμα ἄνθρωπος; Oὔκ· ἀλλ' ἀνθρώπου σῶμα καλεῖται. Eἴπερ οὖν κατ' ἰδίαν μὲν τούτων οὐδέτερον ἄνθρωπός ἐστι, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἀμφοτέρων συμπλοκῆς καλεῖται ἄνθρωπος, κέκληκε δὲ ὁ θεὸς εἰς ζωὴν καὶ ἀνάστασιν τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οὐ τὸ μέρος ἀλλὰ τὸ ὅλον κέκληκεν, ὅπερ ἐστὶ τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ τὸ σῶμα. Ἐπεὶ πῶς οὐκ ἄτοπον, ἀμφοτέρων ὄντων κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ, τὸ μὲν σώζειν, τὸ δὲ μή; Oὐκ ὄντος γὰρ ἀδυνάτου, καθάπερ δέδεικται, τὴν σάρκα ἔχειν τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν, τίς ἡ διάκρισις, ὥστε τὴν μὲν ψυχὴν σώζεσθαι, τὴν δὲ σάρκα μή; Ἢ φθονερὸν ποιοῦσι τὸν θεόν; Ἀλλὰ ἀγαθός ἐστι καὶ σώζεσθαι πάντας θέλει· καὶ δὴ αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ κηρύγματος αὐτοῦ οὐχὶ μόνον ἤκουσεν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν καὶ σὺν αὐτῇ ἡ σάρξ, καὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἀλλ' ἀμφότερα ἐλούσαντο καὶ ἀμφότερα τὴν δικαιοσύνην εἰργάσαντο. Ἀρ' οὖν ἀχάριστον ἢ ἄδικον ἀποφαίνουσι τὸν θεόν, εἰ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων πιστευόντων ἐπ' αὐτὸν τὴν μὲν σώζειν θέλει, τὴν δὲ οὔ; Ναί, φασίν· ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν ψυχή ἐστιν ἄφθαρτος, μέρος οὖσα τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐμφύσημα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὸ ἴδιον καὶ συγγενὲς ἠθέλησεν σῶσαι· ἡ δὲ σὰρξ φθαρτὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ καθάπερ ἡ ψυχή. Eἶτα τίς αὐτῷ χάρις; Καὶ τίς ἐπίδειξις τῆς δυνάμεως καὶ χρηστότητος αὐτοῦ, εἰ τὸ μὲν φύσει σωζόμενον καὶ μέρος ὑπάρχον αὐτοῦ σώζειν ἤμελλεν; Aὐτὸ γὰρ ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ εἶχε τὴν σωτηρίαν, ὥστε τὴν μὲν ψυχὴν σώζων οὐ μέγα ποιεῖ· τὸ γὰρ σώζεσθαι πάρεστιν αὐτῇ, ὅτι ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ μέρος, ἐμφύσημα αὐτοῦ οὖσα. Ἀλλ' οὐδὲ χάρις αὐτῷ τὸ ἴδιον σώζοντι· τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ἑαυτὸν σώζειν. Ὁ γὰρ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ σώζων δι' ἑαυτοῦ ἑαυτὸν σώζει, μή ποτε ἐκεῖνο τὸ μέρος ἐνδεὲς γένηται. Oὐκ ἔστιν ἀγαθοῦ τὸ τοιοῦτον. Oὐδὲ γὰρ ἄνθρωπον ἀγαθόν τις ἐρεῖ τὸν τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐγγόνοις χαριζόμενόν τι. Τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ τὰ ἀγριώτατα τῶν θηρίων ποιοῦσι· κἂν ὑπεραποθανεῖν τῶν ἐκγόνων αὐτῶν δέῃ, ἑκοντὶ τοῦτο ὑπομένουσιν. Eἰ δέ τις τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς δούλοις παράσχοι, δικαίως ἂν οὗτος λέγοιτο ἀγαθός. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ σωτὴρ ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς ἀγαπᾶν τοὺς ἐχθρούς, ἐπεὶ τίς ὑμῖν χάρις; φησίν. Ὥστε δέδειχεν ἡμῖν ἀγαθὸν ἔργον εἶναι τὸ μὴ τοὺς ἐξ αὐτοῦ γεγονότας μόνον ἀγαπᾶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἔξωθεν. Ἂ δὲ ἡμῖν παρήγγειλε πολὺ πρότερον αὐτὸς ἐποίει. ***
pass_a_gloss: Yes, they say; but the flesh is sinful, so that it also forces the soul to sin with it, vainly accusing it and attributing the sins of both to it alone. For where could the flesh sin by itself, if it did not have the soul leading and calling it? Just as when a yoke of oxen is untied from each other, neither of them can plow alone, so also the soul and body, when untied from their yoking, cannot do anything by themselves. But if the flesh alone is sinful, the Savior came for its sake, as he says: I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Since, then, the flesh has been shown to be precious and glorious to God, beyond all his creations, it will rightly be saved by him. We should say to those who claim that, even if the flesh is the best of God's creations and precious to him beyond all else, it does not immediately have the promise of resurrection. And yet, how is it not absurd that what came into being with such great counsel and is precious beyond all else should be neglected by its creator so as to no longer exist? The creator and artist, if they want their images to remain so that they may be glorified through them, restore them when they are decaying; will God, then, neglect his own possession and creation, letting it be as if it did not exist, and not restore it to existence? We call this idle work, just as if someone built a house and then tore it down, or neglected a ruined house when they could restore it; we will not accuse God of doing something in vain. But the imperishable and wise God is not like that. Let the unbelievers praise such a view, if they have it! But in fact, he has called the flesh to resurrection and promises it eternal life. For where he preaches the gospel to save humanity, he preaches it to the flesh as well. What is a human being, if not a rational living being composed of soul and body? Is the soul alone a human being? No, it is the soul of a human being. Is the body alone called a human being? No, it is called the body of a human being. If, then, neither of these is a human being by itself, but the combination of both is called a human being, and God has called the human being to life and resurrection, he has called not the part, but the whole, which is the soul and the body. Since both exist together and in the same way, how is it not absurd to save one and not the other? For it has been shown that the flesh can have rebirth, so what is the distinction, such that the soul is saved, but the flesh is not? Or do they make God envious? But God is good and wants to save all; and in fact, both our soul and our flesh have heard his gospel and believed in Christ Jesus, and both have been cleansed and have worked righteousness. Do they, then, show God to be ungrateful or unjust, if he wants to save one of the two that have believed in him, but not the other? Yes, they say; but the soul is imperishable, being a part of God and his breath, and for this reason he wanted to save it, as it is his own and akin to him; the flesh, however, is perishable and not from him, as the soul is. What, then, is his gratitude? And what is the display of his power and goodness, if he was going to save what is naturally saved and is a part of him? For it had salvation from him, since it is his part, his breath; so saving the soul is not a great deed. But neither is it a favor to save what is his own; for this is to save himself. The one who saves his own part is saving himself, lest that part become lacking. This is not characteristic of a good person. For no one would call a person good who shows favor to their own children and descendants; even the wildest of beasts do this, and they would even die for their offspring. If someone shows the same favor to their slaves, they would rightly be called good. That is why the Savior taught us to love our enemies, since what favor is there in that? He says. So he showed us that it is a good work to love not only those who come from him, but also those outside. What he commanded us to do, he did first.

choices.why: The Greek word ἀναγκάζειν means to compel or force someone to do something.
The Greek word συζυγία refers to the act of yoking or joining two things together.
The Greek word παλιγγενεσία refers to the act of being born again or rebirth.

pass_b_english: Yes, they say, but the flesh is sinful, so that it forces the soul to sin along with it, accusing the soul in vain and laying the sins of both upon it alone. For where could the flesh sin by itself, if it did not have the soul leading and inciting it? Just as when a yoke of oxen is untied from the yoke, neither ox can plow by itself, so also soul and body, when separated from their union, can do nothing by themselves. But if the flesh alone is sinful, the Savior came for its sake, as he says: "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Matthew 9:13). Since, then, the flesh has been shown to be precious to God and glorious beyond all his works, it will rightly be saved by him. We must say to those who claim that, even if the flesh is the very best of God's creations and precious to him above all else, it does not at once possess the promise of the resurrection. And yet, how is it not absurd that what came into being with such great counsel and is precious beyond all the rest should be neglected by its maker so as to cease to exist? A potter and painter, if they want the images they make to endure so that they may be glorified through them, restore them when they decay; would God, then, overlook his own possession and creation, letting it be as nothing, and no longer restore it to existence? We call this idle labor, just as if someone built a house and then tore it down, or looked on a ruined house when able to rebuild it; we would not blame a man for doing something in vain. But the imperishable God is not such a one, nor is the mind of the universe foolish by nature. Let the unbelievers speak well of such a view, if unbelief is what they possess! But in fact he has called the flesh to the resurrection and promises it eternal life. For where he proclaims the gospel to save the human being, he proclaims it to the flesh as well. What is a human being, if not a rational living creature composed of soul and body? Is the soul by itself a human being? No, it is the soul of a human being. Is the body by itself called a human being? No, it is called the body of a human being. If, then, neither of these is a human being by itself, but the human being is called the combination of both, and God has called the human being to life and resurrection, he has called not the part but the whole, which is the soul and the body. Since both exist together and in the same way, how is it not absurd to save the one and not the other? For it has been shown that the flesh can have the rebirth, so what is the distinction, such that the soul is saved but the flesh is not? Or do they make God envious? But God is good and wants to save all; and indeed both our soul and our flesh have heard his gospel and believed in Christ Jesus, and both have been washed and both have worked righteousness. Do they, then, show God to be ungrateful or unjust, if he wants to save the one of the two that have believed in him, but not the other? Yes, they say; but the soul is imperishable, being a part of God and his breath, and for this reason he willed to save it, as it is his own and akin to him; the flesh, however, is perishable and not from him, as the soul is. What, then, is his gratitude? And what is the display of his power and goodness, if he was going to save what is saved by nature and is a part of him? For it had salvation from itself, since it is his part, his breath; so saving the soul is no great deed. But neither is it a favor for him to save what is his own; for this is to save himself. The one who saves his own part saves himself through himself, lest that part become lacking. This is not the character of a good person. For no one would call a human being good who shows favor to their own children and descendants; even the wildest of beasts do this, and they would even die for their offspring. If someone shows the same favor to their slaves, they would rightly be called good. That is why the Savior taught us to love our enemies, since what favor is there in that? he says. So he showed us that it is a good work to love not only those who come from him, but also those outside. What he commanded us to do, he did first.
